DIF now allows individual contributors without being members. As Rouven
pointed out in an earlier email currently DIF members (Associate members) and individuals who signed
the Feedback Agreement can participate in the work carried out by the WG.
(please note, Feedback Agreement should be signed by individuals who only represent themselves and
they could- and should not represent any of their employers. Preferably only freelancers)
Please send this form to the folks who already meet the individual contributor requirements  and ask them to complete the DocuSign sent after submitting the
form.
Additionally, please connect me with the companies who are not individuals and let me share with
them the WG charter and pre-explain them the IPR release etc. related to WG contributions so
they can sign the release forms as soon as we figured out the legal aspects, as described
below.
Related to your ask and the community's signals we started to look into ways to open up certain
Working Groups to allow free company contributions as well. It requires additional legal and
accounting work therefore it will take another 1-3 weeks until we can announce the changes. The
current goal is to open up WGs for contributing companies for free. At least I can promise that
we will make sure that even if not all WGs gets open IDWG will have the same participation
arrangement as the Secure Data Storage WG.

2022-03-03T14:32:16.000Z
Good Morning Folks-
As we move to harden KERIpy for a production implementation of the vLEI ecosystem, we (mostly Sam) analyzed our approach to rotation events for distributed multisig identifiers. In particular, our support for partial rotations (rotating with only a subset of all signers that still satisfies the signature threshold) came under scrutiny.
The result was the following issue and subsequent PR addressing the issue. In short, we changed the format for the `n` field and added an `nt` field for all establishment events to support partial rotations. The HackMD referenced in this issue has details of the new events and the issue itself details the logic needed to ensure a secure partial rotation.
2022-03-03T14:33:20.000Z
The PR is also referenced in the issue if you want to see the implementation in KERIpy along with all the test vectors that broke as a result. :smirk:

<@U024CJMG22J>, here are my next set of questions, prefaced with assumptions:
*Assumptions*:
1) Provenant platform will create a hosted cloud wallets in AWS for entity’s
2) Provenant platform will use delegated keys to act on behalf of the holders of the wallets
*Questions*:
1) Since private keys need to be stored in an entity’s (hosted) wallet, should the entity’s inception event happen after the wallet is created and run on the server where the wallet is stored?
2) Does the Provenant platform, on behalf of an entity, need to supply the AID to the QVI for it to issue a vLEI to the entity?
3) Who makes the request for a vLEI?
4) When a QVI issues a vLEI to an entity, how does the entity receive the credential offer?
5) GLEIF uses a GLEIF delegated key to issue vLEIs to QVIs, does it also give QVIs a GLEIF delegated key or do QVIs use their own private key to sign credentials they issue?
6) Can a delegated key be created from a delegated key? Who approves the delegated key of a delegated key?
7) Does a request for a delegated key result in a new AID and pair of keys for the delegatee? If yes, does that mean that the delegatee needs a wallet?
8) Please confirm that pre-rotated keys and delegated keys are stored in the holder’s wallet in the secure key storage along with the private key
9) Does an entity with a Validating Agent role need a vLEI? Or does the Validating Agent only vet entities and work with LOUs to issue LEIs?
2022-03-08T18:29:31.000Z
10) If a wallet is created before an inception event, how is the wallet associated with an entity? Is it by the friendly name of the wallet?
2022-03-08T20:39:09.000Z
1. Yes, creation of an identifier occurs after the database and keystore is created. From the command line tool, you run `kli init` first and `kli incept` afterwards.
2. There are detailed flows for identity assurance and identifier exchange as part of the vLEI ecosystem. Those need to be followed to ensure secure communication on which the credential issuance is based.
3. There are designated representatives for a Legal Entity who are authorized to request any of the credentials from a QVI
4. There is a credential issuance peer to peer protocol define as a series of `exn` messages. The holder will receive a `exn` message with a `/credential/issue` route.
5. Private keys are never shared with KERI. Each QVI will create an identifier that is delegated from the GLEIF External AID. So the QVI has its own keys for its identifier with is delegated from GLEIF.
6. Yes, a new identifier can specify a key that is also a delegate as its delegator. So it would look like A -> B -> C where A is B's delegator and B is C's delegator. To authorize an establishment event of a delegate, a delegator needs to anchor the establishment event in either an interaction (`ixn`) or a rotation (`rot`) event. So in B's case, she could authorize C's events with an `ixn` event and not require any further action from A. But is B wants to use `rot` events to anchor C's events, those events would have to be verified by A with a corresponding anchor.
7. Yes, a delegate needs its own wallet and holds its own keys. The delegate initiates its own AID, specifying the AID to use as its delegator.
8. All private keys (current and next) are stored in the secure key storage, yes.
9. Validating Agents are part of LEIs and not vLEIs so they won't need vLEI credentials
10. A wallet is merely the database and keystore. An identifier created for that wallet has all its key material stored in the keystore and yes, it is given a user friendly name so human's can remember what it is later.

FYI:
CEN/CLC/JTC19 has approved a work item aiming to produce a Technical Specification with the following title: "Decentralised Identity Management Model based on Blockchain and other Distributed Ledgers Technologies. –Part 1: Generic Reference Framework".As per document N 103, the scope of the work item is the following: "The proposed standard will specify a reference architecture for decentralised identity management, optionally enabled by distributed ledger technology (DLT) and blockchain systems. The reference architecture aims to natural persons and legal entities and addresses concepts, cross-cutting aspects, architectural considerations, and architecture views, including functional components, roles, activities, and their relationships with blockchain and DLT.

2022-06-30T17:14:47.000Z
Now that the `keripy` development team has finished the big push to complete the vLEI XBRL Annual Report Signing Pilot (see press release here: ) we are updating the branches and development process to live up to our commitment to have a more stable `main` branch in our repository.
We just renamed our primary branch from `master` to `main` and then created the `development` branch which will be used for all active development moving forward. Any PRs should be submitted against `development` and we, as a community will agree when it is time to cut a next release from `development` and merge all outstanding changes into `main`. We will commit to ensuring that all unit tests, demo scripts, command line commands and REST APIs will work as advertised at all times on the `main` branch moving forward. (There will be a series of PRs over the next week or so to get us there).
If you have already cloned or forked the `keripy` repo, you can run the following commands to update your local copy of the primary branch from `master` to `main`.
git branch -m master main
git fetch origin
git branch -u origin/main main
git remote set-head origin -aOf course changing `origin` to whatever your remote is named for the `WebOfTrust/keripy` remote repository.

2022-07-13T14:42:41.000Z
Hi Lance, for what I’ve understood is that Ledger-registered backers are a secondary root-of-trust at best. It’s an extra guarantee. The primary root of trust is the KEL, which is cryptographically verifiable to this primary root-of-trust (PKI). Afaik KERI doesn’t organize portability between two ledger-registered backers (from one ledger to another), However, KERI is a portable autonomic identifier system in itself by design, and you’re free to use as many blockchains as you like to create secondary roots of trusts. But how efficient or useful that’ll be….
Phil definitely has a better thorough understanding of KERI and all of its technicalities. But this is my take on it, feel free to correct me if I am wrong (because I might well be :slightly_smiling_face: )

2022-07-13T16:13:09.000Z
Interesting, Lance, I’ll follow your efforts. Here again my two cents:
The problem with a ledger being the single root-of-trust for a witness (if I understand your idea correctly) is that its key are not rotatable. You’d need a transaction on the ledger to rotate the controlling key of the witness, which leaves you locked in: not portable anymore (locked to the silo / blockchain of this specific ledger), it’s become algoritmic identifier not an autonomic one. I believe KERI needs AID based witnesses to be able to offer KERI’s
• security model: duplicity detection and reconciliation
• features: portable identifiers, secure attribution over the web

2022-08-05T12:08:44.000Z
<@U02PA6UQ6BV>: I had a look at your terms wiki. Very impressive work, and I think this will be immensely valuable to the entire community.
I turned on automatic glossary generation for the wiki, and configured it slightly. Here is the URL for the glossary that goes with your terms wiki:
Notice that when you hover over a term, there's an icon at the left that allows you to link to a specific term. When you click the icon, it copies onto your clipboard a link to that term. For example, here's the term "digital signature":
I noticed a few things about the data on the wiki pages that was making the glossary sub-optimal, so I fixed things here and there. Some things you might check if something doesn't render the way you want:
1. Images as displayed in raw wiki markdown have a different canvas size than images in the glossary. For this reason, it is often best to force images to be a specific size that will be good for the glossary. You can see how I've done this in the wiki page for authentic chained data container, for example:
2022-08-05T12:10:01.000Z
2. The headers for additional sections of your wiki page should not be more indented than the header for Definition. If Definition begins with two hashes: `## Definition`, then subsequent sections should also begin with 2. If they don't, then the glossary generation may only display the more indented content.

2022-10-11T21:46:34.000Z
Hey Folks, sorry about the delayed responses, Sam is on vacation, I am dealing with family issues and Kevin is taking up all the slack with GLEIF and our go live date of November 1st.
2022-10-11T21:47:46.000Z
I'll give an over all witness description here and then try to answer specific questions where they were asked.
2022-10-11T21:56:44.000Z
Each witness is independent and keeps local copies of all KELs that they know about. We have not implement gossip protocols yet so as an alternative we have implemented the policy that all controllers are responsible for propagating their key events to all their witnesses and then pass out all receipts from each witness to the other witnesses. In addition, the controller is also responsible for introducing witnesses to each other when a controller uses them together. This eliminates the need to bootstrap any kind of witness introduction while we don't have gossip implemented.
Gossip is dependent on UDP protocol support which is dependent on CESR streaming of events themselves which Sam has started but not finished because revised rotation rules has taken precedence. Once we pop that stack and have gossip working, witness (and watcher) communication will be simplified. But for now, keripy controllers make sure to introduce all witnesses to each other (admittedly a little chatty), sends events to each witness, collect all receipts from each witness and then send them back out to the other witnesses.
2022-10-11T22:10:30.000Z
As for HTTP vs TCP. Witnesses do expose a TCP port which will work fine for direct streaming of KERI events. However, the keripy agent and command line exclusively use CESR streaming over HTTP.
2022-10-11T22:11:27.000Z
The reason is that we had to focus on HTTP in order to support mailboxes for controllers that do not have persistent Internet connection and that was built using HTTP.
2022-10-11T22:16:57.000Z
So all the configuration we use currently favors HTTP for all communication
2022-10-11T23:55:24.000Z
Thanks a lot <@U024CJMG22J> . I have no rush on any answer. I just throw here so other can catch up as well.
2022-10-11T23:57:08.000Z
One more conceptual question regarding witnesses based on what you said: can a witness witness more than one agent at the same time?
2022-10-12T00:00:29.000Z
Yes, the current witness implementation in keripy is promiscuous. As long as a controller commits to a witness in its KEL, the witness will provide a signed receipt. It is assumed that any deployment of witnesses will provide authentication over their witnesses to prevent them from witnessing for any AID.
2022-10-12T00:04:42.000Z
Fair. At least for an implementation point of view I like the idea of having a witness validating multiple KELs.
2022-10-12T00:07:37.000Z
Non-transferable identifiers and receipting key events are both so cheap, witness infrastructure can be deployed to support any configuration you need. Whether that is multiple AIDs using the same witness AID or one for one AID to witness AID, the protocol should scale to any level.
2022-10-12T00:08:30.000Z

2022-10-24T09:00:38.000Z
Hi all,
I have a couple of questions about credentials
1. Are there plans for supporting querying credentials by attribute value or metadata parameters? For example letting a credential issuer query issued credentials by LEI code or by date of issuance?
2. Semantics of OOR and ECR authorization credentials. Who issues OOR and ECR authorization credentials and who is the recipient? What values will be set in personLegalName, officialRole and engagementContextRole attributes of the authorization credential?
3. Extending credential schema. For example how can I extend ECR credential schema with an email attribute?
4. Credential expiration. The roles that OOR and ECR credentials represent often have a known end date based on some business contract for example. Is there a way to set expiration date on these credentials?
Thanks!
2022-10-24T09:00:38.000Z
I want to know these answers as well. Good questions. Here’s my understanding from what the KERI whitepaper and IETF specs say:
1) querying credentials by metadata is supported and querying by value is part of the graduated disclosure mechanism so yes, support exists or is planned for both.
2)looks like VLEI specific credential types. Only a vLEI expert can answer completely. I suspect either a QVI or a company itself issues both of those types. Don’t take my word for it. I imagine the values are context specific. If you are looking for a type system to select from a distinct set of values there may be a specification somewhere that constrains those values. Otherwise the values are up to the issuer.
3) extending the credential schema should be doable by adding another ACDC linked to the original as ACDCs are an extensible graph structure.
4) there’s a way to set the expiration date on any credential since an expiration date is a regular property of a credential. Regardless of an expiration date you will want to verify control authority for a credential by verifying KELs.
My understanding is that only a QVI can issue an OOR, but it requires an AUTH credential () from the Legal Entity to the QVI; the Legal Entity must hold a valid Legal Entity vLEI credential.
I believe the ECR can be issued by either the Legal Entity or by a QVI if the Legal Entity issues an AUTH credential () to the QVI. In either case the Legal Entity must hold a valid Legal Entity vLEI credential.

2022-11-18T15:23:52.000Z
Due to recent activities in keri community and some uncertainties have arisen in regards of the license of Human Colossus Foundation implementation would like to provide you some insights. As you all know HCF have very specific strategy regarding protecting the community and the implementation which we are working on. We invested already quite some resources and money into what we have build. Our vision could be described as: building with community for the community. Based on that we did quite in deep evaluation of different licensing options and we ended up (in our opinion) with one of the best option which is EUPL1.2. I know that a lot of people do not have a good understanding of that part and sometimes misinterpret the consequences of the license. This is why we prepared short summary of our reasoning and argumentation why we pick EUPL and why it matters for us.
Here you can find it:
I would love to here everyone take on that and prepare questions if you have any.
As you know as HCF we are working on many components of KERI ecosystem and we are pretty advance in it, including keriox, cesrox and said all that is already separated, and is used in multiple projects. Obviously we don't mind if that work would be duplicated because you would find a good reason to not go with EUPL license. But as far as I know there is no reason to do so. And if someone would be able to prove benefits of other license for those components which fulfills our demands we are willing to change that license for benefits of community. Until that would happen, we would protect our community investment in a way as described above.
I already requested to have a slot on the KERI call to provide some more insights and hear everyone opinion in that regards and eventually address some of those questions. If everything goes right we would have a chance to speak on next KERI Call but before hand feel free to provide your feedback and post questions in this thread.
Best regards
Head of Technology Council at Human Colossus Foundation

Is the best start for building an authentication system and authorization system using KERI?
I am mapping the KERI protocol onto a traditional sign-in and authorization model.
It seems that the sign-in would be replaced with a profile acknowledgment based on a stored credential in some local browser storage that then personalized a user’s experience.
This requires a web wallet or web data satchel (help me name this). Do we have any examples of storing credentials or keypairs in indexeddb? I know it’s not the best solution though I’m just doing a POC prototype.
If there are no examples then it seems all I need to do for a web is the following:
1. The ability to create, store, and recover a keypair, inception and rotation,
2. The ability to send messages to witnesses and store receipts
3. The ability to view stored credentials and
4. to send existing credentials (graduated disclosure)
5. The ability to issue new credentials
6. The ability to sign events, or respond to signing challenges.
I’m still reading through the SKWA document so maybe it covers many of these points.

2022-11-18T22:06:03.000Z
By ‘activities and uncertainties’ I mean that people are not sure how the know-how brought by HCF can be reused and how we can collaborate since we under another license. A lot of people treat EUPL as GPL which leads to wrong assumption.
Yes we (and Jolocom) contributed keriox to weboftrust as the work started on Apache 2 and we didn't wanted just simply pull that from DIF. We decided to switch to EUPL for better protection of the community behind it. What was already done stays under that license we cannot withdraw it or at least won't be nice to try to hid it anyway.
I am fine with two project under different license. We have strong arguments why we chose the EUPL - mainly to protect the community and avoid situation that private company would pick it and extend it without sharing back, causing forks and split of the community or even the protocols. It is beneficial for whole community if we would continue use EUPL. But as I said it is our world view and complete understand if other would take thoughtful decision based on facts and not just false assumption.
We are investing quite a lot into the development of those components and I bet that other community members would like to do that as well. Doing it twice it is just a bit of wast resources especially if there would not be any good argument for that.
Especially that we are almost done with cesrox as a separate package.

2022-11-19T20:54:21.000Z
Completely agree that lengthy and complicated licenses does not help regular users to jump on board. But keep in mind that in many cases licenses like that does not have any grounding in the real law. For individual person maybe that is not very important but when you deal with businesses or governmental services you can't simply skip that bit.
Or define "do good not evil" - good for whom, what means good?. If you face serious business and face their legal department you would bounce of it relatively quickly.
Community needs support to navigate through this space anyway. This is why we team up with lawyers to make sure that we get it right and we are able to protect our community in the right way. Through our experience we went through many open source communities and initiatives and personal must say that I am feed up with the direction which this takes. "Open Source" become marketing tool, nobody think about collaboration and community, Big tech companies used that to warm up their image. It lead to a trap called "platforms" and providing free development force for those who actually can monetize specific technology. You use open source and think that your are independent because you have control over code but you are under control of corporate machine. One of many examples is android as OS which is great open source OS but actually without using google services this operating system is useless and not user friendly, You can NOT have simple push notification in your own "open source" app running on open source service, using open source backend without google having stake in that.
Decentralization is not only about technology it is as well about governance and distribution of power. Letting everyone do what ever they want (more permissive licensing) is not always good for what we do.

Is there a specific message for a witness to tell the agent that its ley events won’t be witnessed?
2022-11-23T22:47:40.000Z
I haven’t heard of this though I’m looking it up. Will you ask this on Stackoverflow? The KERI tag has no questions:
Let’s get that tag started! I’ll post my answer here and there.
A message is the closest kind of event I could find that might serve this purpose. Nothing else jumps out at me yet. It would seem odd that a witness would refuse to witness a controller’s key events given that the controller can select its own witnesses. The following quote from section 10.2 *Indirect Replay Mode* of the white paper illustrates this fact:
> _The reliance on a designated set of witnesses provides several advantages. The first is that the_
> _identifier’s trust basis is not locked to any given witness or set of witnesses but may be transferred_
> _at the controller’s choosing._
So, given that a controller selects its own witnesses it is the responsibility of the controller to validate the suitability of each witness prior to including that witness in an inception or rotation event as a declared witness.
As a part of the witness evaluation process I could see value in adding a protocol-level event for a given KERI agent (witness, watcher, juror, judge) to indicate it is not able to or will refuse to be a witness for a given controller, though this delves into business-process specific decisions that are likely bespoke to a given implementation and thus don’t yet make sense to add to KERI itself.
I asked because a witness may stop responding and will be up to the controlled to check why. However the witness may have valid reasons that can be communicated directly (lack of resources, unpaid service, etc)
for example, are the GLEIF production witnesses willing to accept KEL from any agent? what about a spasm?

This is how HCF was created. So far we where able to unify all above into one stack and linking all technologies created in different place (contributing in those places in the same time) into what you would call GUT. If you didn't I recommend to read introduction to DDE Stack:
We continue sharing and promoting our achievements in all mentioned communities but we know how hard is to break the ice in a way to think about certain things and hard to enforce it. Based on our experience just following Unix philosophy is more then enough and helps with adoption. This is how we were able to introduce OCA into Aries ecosystem and same way we are building keri components (cesr, sai, tel and more). Happy to hear your experience and understand the reasoning.

2023-02-03T04:24:07.000Z
One of the "why" questions I have to answer is "why did Sam create something new (CESR) instead of using what we already have (CBOR, COSE, Multi-Codec)?"
The answer is very clear to me now. We believe that all data in the future will need to be authentic data and therefore, cryptographic primitives (AIDs, key digests, signatures) will be included with every bit of data transmitted and stored across the internet. Those primitives must be represented as strings and not data structures to ensure we are able to ship the most compact form of those primitives. CESR is the only encoding format that enables us to ship cryptographic primitives as first class encoded strings that are more compact than CBOR structures of the same data and even more compact when shipped as binary.
2023-02-03T04:25:57.000Z
When you look at the size of that public key and signature that we will have to use to be post-quantum secure you can see why this is so important.

2023-02-05T11:30:00.000Z
Last ACDC meeting, near the end, Daniel asked a question and I came up with a potential solution to it by concatenating two identifiers to form a single one. The idea was that a namespace would be hashed to provide the first part of the identifier, and a complete data structure to provide the rest. I’ll now give a complete description that I believe will create an auto-governing system, potentially addressing Phil’s concern. Sorry for not using the typical one letter identifiers, I don’t know them off the top so I’m going to be verbose so that I can communicate clearly.
namespace: {
digest: "E...",
name: "xyz.qui.domain.identifier",
issuer: "did:keri:E.."
}
digest: "E...",
version: "0.1.0",
// other data
}
If we combine (`namespace.digest` | `digest`), we can create a fixed-length searchable (by digest of issuer and name) versioning system where only the identified issuer can create versions of their data. There is no administration required, I believe. The trick is that `issuer` is an input to `namespace.digest`, and `namespace.digest` is an input to `digest` (we could use a compact expression of this information). The caveats:
• to allow this data to enter such a system, one needs it to be signed by the issuer
• to prevent abuse, one needs to ensure that one has the ability to throttle/cap by issuer id (unless, I suppose, resources are unconstrained?)
• consumers would be pulling _all_ versions for a given `name`/`issuer` pair
Is this new/useful/flawed?

A small _side step_: Validate, verify, validator en verifier are terms we might have to reiterate now and again. In our domain (KERI/ACDC) we seem to be able to work within the broader eSSIF-lab definitions. Mind you, the __ definition is very general, in the KERI/ACDC vocabulary ‘validate’ currently has diverse meanings including this one.
(general)
**, of determining whether or not that data is valid to be used for some specific purpose(s) of that **.
**, of determining whether that data is *authentic* (i.e. originates from the ** that authored it), timely (i.e. has not expired), and conforms to other specifications that apply to its structure.
In the KERI/ACDC domain we have come here:
If your border case / criterium is authenticity, as one could understand from “Validated meaning there is some signed chain going back to a root that validates the issuer as a member”, then first part of the sentence is what a verifier in KERI/ACDC in a narrow sense does, the second part ‘validate as a member’ is more a validator’s role.
Example: You keypass of the hotel might verify, the doorman might still not validate you as a guest allowed inside (validation).
It’s all about what we as a group collectively understand how individual members look at the criteria to draw lines between closely related terms in our terminology, even if borders between certain terms are vague. At the same time it would come in very handy if the outside world, outside of KERI/ACDC would still know what we’re talking about.
“I first have to try to understand what you mean, and then we might enjoy the bliss of reversal.”
I pass the baton back to Phil / Jason.

2023-02-12T22:18:01.000Z
KERI is a protocol developed by Dr Sam Smith, keripy is the reference implementation of that protocol.
There is a white paper and draft IETF specification along with it.
CESR, ACDC, PTEL, SAID are all derivatives that have been extracted from, or developed from the original white paper by Sam or <@U024CJMG22J> primarily, it’s open source so obviously there are other contributions.
There is no one over arching organization, that’s the great thing, we get contributions from a variety of companies.
<@U04HQD29Z7E> has a good point, there was a split over the introduction of a European copy left license for a variety of reasons.
Sams original idea was to use IETF to harbor specifications and Apache2 to foster implementations.
His reasoning he documented in the WebOfTrust/keri readme I believe.
Welcome! Hopefully we can answer any questions you have.

2023-02-12T23:11:10.000Z
We have started from scratch with cesr/parside, the short version is: CESR is a sub spec of keri and is often deemed the “hard bit” to implement making adoption harder.
We decided to start from scratch and model closer to keripy (which fully implements cesr) than what was previously out there.
As Sam continues to develop cesr, keripy will likely remain the spearhead of development, libraries downstream (in my opinion) will benefit from being closer to keripy (harboring a common vernacular etc)
2023-02-12T23:14:26.000Z
Do not discount the THC work though if you’re looking at rust, they have a very comprehensive write up on their license and why.
So again it depends on what you’re doing.

2023-02-19T02:27:56.000Z
I am reading the KERI white paper and came across the fact that KEL is considered a secondary root of trust (Page 60/141, Section 7.35).
In my understanding (which seems to be wrong), the controller of a transferrable AID—where the inception key is already rotated—needs both the current signing key and a KEL to cryptographically prove their control authority over the AID. Hence, my previous understanding was that the AID together with its KEL acts collectively as the primary root of trust.
I would really appreciate it if someone is willing to clarify this point.
Number of replies: 14
2023-02-19T02:27:56.000Z
It is important to remember that KERI's security is based on the layering of thresholds. The whole is greater than the sum of it's parts.
So while it seems that with a transferable identifier (one that can be rotated), the security of the identifier starts with its KEL, it does not.
As with all identifier types (transferable and non-transferable), the security starts with entropy. The randomness used to create the private key is the absolute root of trust. Once you create the private key you retain the ability to prove control over your identifier by your ability to use the private key.
With non-transferable identifiers, it ends there. With transferable identifiers, the next root of trust (and thus a secondary root of trust) is the KEL which provides the ability to rotate the keys of the identifier.
Additional roots-of-trust layered on top of entropy and KELs include multi-sig support, delegation and witnesses.

In every cryptographic system entropy rules, and if you don't use a good rng (a csprng) you're boned from the start. This is really important for everyone in the space to understand. I knew a guy who was really into measuring hamming weights of outputs for everything he did as a crude way of ensuring sufficient entropy in the things he built.
I mostly used random generators that came from main crypto libraries. How can we know if there are good or not. Is there a list of libraries that we should consider using in out projects, or a list of the ones that we should never use?
Generally you want to use the one supplied by the operating system. In linux this used to be `/dev/urandom` I believe but there was another one that wasn't cryptographic (the tradeoff must be speed, I've never read about it though I have implemented a prng or two).
In Rust you typically use `OsRng` from the random crate in fashion. In `cesride` we rely on two variants due to the expectations of `ed25519-dalek` and `k256`, and we simply pass them to the libraries to generate keys. You'd need to investigate how to get random bits in whatever language you are using, and just make sure what you are reading is about a `csprng` and not just an `rng` or `prng`.
This looks like it has a lot of good info, though I'm a bit lazy about reading it today:
And, even a good `csprng` should be seeded well - if you can get random data from measuring user input or environmental conditions that can't be easily controlled you will generally be more resistant to attack. Think about the case for example, where a designer is tempted to use a radio receiver and noise to seed the RNG, but an attacker floods the space with a frequency that produces a deterministic result in the ADC or something.

Good discussion, I conclude that urandom is at least a PRNG. I’ve created this stuff:
and entries in the Q-and-A.
Here's a way to view entropy on the command line (should work in Linux and macOS):
```cat /dev/urandom | od -tx1 -Ax```
if you want a specific number of bytes, something like:
```dd if=/dev/urandom bs=1 count=32 > entropy
cat entropy | od -tx1 -Ax```
I'd also recommend trying out WSL2 in Windows if you are unfamiliar, for a more consistent dev experience across platforms - you should have `urandom` in there too.
In KERIpy we use libsodium through the python bindings. I've never actually looked at what their documentation says about randomness, but here it is:
> The library provides a set of functions to generate unpredictable data, suitable for creating secret keys.
> • On Windows systems, the `RtlGenRandom()` function is used.
> • On OpenBSD and Bitrig, the `arc4random()` function is used.
> • On recent FreeBSD and Linux kernels, the `getrandom` system call is used.
> • On other Unices, the `/dev/urandom` device is used.
Thought that was interesting based on this conversation.

vsuvorov
2023-03-08T11:56:23.000Z
I believe he's simply referring to the fact that various cryptographic primitives can be used. Such as various hash methods or signatures.
The danger of cryptographic agility is simply that libraries can be poorly implemented and not follow proper verification logic. Which was famously the case with JOSE/JWTs ( e.g. headers are ). Another gotcha is that people will use poor choices when configuring keys, selecting algorithms, etc. That's what `nacl` is helping to avoid. Or `paseto` tokens, etc.
Lastly, it adds complexity to the processing logic and therefore potential bugs, including side channels. See TLS crypto suits ( e.g. downgrade attacks).
From my standpoint ( and I'm not a cryptographer) KERI is using cryptographic agility justifiably:
• new type or stronger key algos can be used in the future for transferable prefixes.
• the set of primitives is relatively small and is easy to reason about.
I think so too. I still don’t understand why he explicit puts GLEIF in the spotlight for this; there are thousands of projects that meet those criteria (even better). Why GLEIF.
I guess it's because GLEIF is a high profile project which is also a first mover to adapt a brand new cryptography based tech ( cryptographers are usually highly suspicious of any new efforts in that space).
And he's probably biased towards , which arguably targets the same space and challenges as KERI/ACDC. :)
I think Vasily is correct here. He is confusing KERI's support of cryptographic agility, which means support for multiple algorithms with the problems JOSE had because they allowed flexibility is selection of parameters for specific algorithms. The later allowed for downgrading security by making poor choices in the parameters.

Imagine these two scenarios to start:
1. You want to purchase a bottle of wine and need to prove your age, but your driver's license contains all kinds of information you'd rather not share with the staff. Instead of giving them an id, you scan a QR code on their device and begin OOBI with the seller, and begin an exchange process of graduated and selective disclosure that ensure that if you have a credential or ACDC with appropriate chain of authority (back to something like a governmental body) proving you are 19, proof of this and your authentic, unexpired id photo is presented for verification by the employee via the exchange. Their system allows them to approve the sale, and you haven't disclosed your address etc.
2. You are arriving at the hospital and dread filling out forms. No need! With ACDCs issued via KERI and their associated records, proven authentic and signed by doctors and institutions, you can enter the hospital without filling any kind of forms.

Those are great examples. I have thought of many more scenarios as well. It’s roughly starting to take shape.
The way you described the “Alcoholic Beverage Age Proof” made it sound a little like the OpenID/OAuth workflow — where interacting with a third party consists of:
#1) Choose an Identity Provider you want to use for interaction.
#2) Sign-in to chosen Identity Provider.
#3) “Review and Accept”, or “Review and Select” what data that will be exposed to the third party.
Whereas, the KERI SSI flow would be something like:
#1) Choose the KERI SSI option as an Identity Provider (no need to sign in, because your keys will be used). Then, if I have never completed the “Alcoholic Beverage Age Proof” with this vendor, I must:
#2) Choose an “Age Disclosure” from a list of acceptable options for providing my age.
#3) Choose a “Photo Disclosure” from a list of acceptable options for providing my photo.
Where, for each disclosure, the third party has pre-selected the “list of acceptable” providers for their specific trust/reputation tolerance level.
Also, the first time you do this, your choices are saved (as an ACDC?), so the next time these disclosures are presented, you will not need to select them again. And the process will end with #1, making for a better user experience.
Additionally, any other third party that requires an “Age Disclosure” or “Photo Disclosure” and accepts the providers chosen will automatically resolve. Again, resulting in a better user experience.
At least, that is what I would imagine.

2023-04-14T22:19:02.000Z
I want to improve and simplify the process of agents discovering each other so connecting across KERI agents can be intuitive from a UX perspective for non-techies.
I am trying to simplify the user experience of connecting KERI Agents to one another and in so doing am looking to automate as much as possible. I want to understand conceptually why I can’t replace the manual OOBI and challenge phrase sharing with a step that is performed by some matchmaking or discovery server.
Essentially I’d like to have a mobile app have a listing of agents pre-loaded so that the user can just tap an agent to connect with, initiate an OOBI exchange, and then a challenge phrase workflow.
What security guarantees do I lose if I have a man-in-the middle matchmaking or discovery service facilitate this? Do I open myself up to man in the middle attacks or is everything still reasonably secure since OOBI resolution results in key state verification, which cannot be faked?
2023-04-14T22:19:02.000Z
You are simply providing a discovery mechanism so as long as each user resolves the OOBI (and verifies key state for themselves) and then does a challenge response you have not sacrificed anything.
Oobi is a way to map the AID with the URL where you can query the end verifiable kel. You can have those pairs in a DB or any place without decreasing security.
But you are changing the dynamic of OOBI exchange. You are asking people to publish an OOBI which eliminates the ability to have 1-1 connections. Not sure that helps anyone but public identifiers for thing like brands.
And that you still need to find a way to share the AID and the challenge words
Thanks Phil, this makes sense.

2023-04-21T01:45:50.000Z
I was recommended to read this article at IIW. It seems there is a disagreement on whether to include specific did methods in the spec. One of the motivations that makes me adopt KERI is to avoid this mess entirely and just use AIDs.
“Summary of Technical Objection
Having the DID WG standardize specific DID methods creates moral hazards that will inevitably reduce the decentralization of DIDs themselves. Whichever methods the group chooses will attain unprecedented acceleration and impact. It will take an increased attention from the WG focused on those methods, taking away from attention that could go to advance all DID methods. That attention will also increase the WGs familiarity with how chosen methods solve certain problems and those approaches will necessarily already have the blessing of the WG, making them preferred favorites over approaches used by other methods. In short, giving the DID WG the permission to focus its attention on selected favorites would directly undermine its ability to advance the work with equal respect for all methods.”

2023-05-02T16:18:10.000Z
new thread about IRL credentials
Number of replies: 18
2023-05-02T16:18:10.000Z
As discussed on today's KERI call, here is an initial PR for a schema for credentials of this type. I'd love further discussion.
7moshe7
When someone identifies himself with an ID card, some devices check if the card is fake. Shouldn't it be worth adding to the schema an option to add "the credibility of the certificate was checked by device X"? Allows adding a choice of guarantee level of reliability.
<@U02MD0HA7EJ>: it's not clear to me what certificate you are referencing. Are you saying that the credential we issue should have a field that records one or more device checks of that very credential?
I meant, apart from the person who checked the person's identity face to face against a passport for example, an optional field *validation machine*, where the name is written and the type of machine X checked the passport itself as not fake (which allows confirmation that the passport itself with which the person identified himself is not fake)
Certificate refers to a passport or any official ID of a person
The field is relevant, in case the entity you are identifying yourself to is not satisfied with the confirmation of your face-to-face identification by a third party, but also wishes to verify that the third party has checked your physical ID by a machine that checks for forgery
<@U03RLLP2CR5> I love the IRL idea and it's relevance to AI phone scams.
Do you envision a way it can be used like Two Factor Authentication on phone calls, email, chat messages?
<@U03KLB48Q2E>: yes, if the risk to eliminate is a risk of non-personhood.
I decided to rename these credentials to "face-to-face credentials" as "IRL credentials" is too dependent on a geeky English acronym. "Face to face" translates into other languages easily, where IRL doesn't.
<@U02MD0HA7EJ>: I have pondered your comments for a couple weeks now, but haven't yet become comfortable with the idea. The reason is that I feel that it encourages a confusion about the purpose of the credentials. But maybe I'm still misunderstanding your vision.
I wrote a markdown file that clarfies the vision/purpose/use cases of the credentials a bit. See /face-to-face/index.md ()
I think the field you're imagining might be called something like `machineCheck?`? You described its relevance by referencing a face-to-face identification and imagined that the issuer has checked the issuee's physical ID. However, I don't imagine that an issuer does any identity checking at all before issuing this credential. That's because the purpose of an IRL credential has little to do with identification. The credential is supposed to prove that the issuee is a human, NOT to prove the human issuee's identity.
I did put an optional field in the schema (`knownAs`) that would allow the issuer to say, "here's a name that I use to interact with the issuee" -- but if it's used, the issuer is not claiming that the name is legally correct or that it's an identifier others should trust or use -- only that it's something they themselves use. So if Alice and Bob meet at a conference, and Alice issues Bob an IRL credential, she could say that the issuee is `knownAs` "BobTheIncredible" to her, because that's what his nametag said -- but she wouldn't care at all whether that was his legal name or just a nickname he felt like scribbling on a nametag. The vital thing she has to check is that the party receiving this credential is a human.
I also put an optional field in the schema for `confirmedHandles` . This is supposed to list email addresses or social media handles that the issuer has used to communicate with the issuee. Perhaps this overlaps a little bit with identification, clouding the purpose of the credential? However, if someone is a work colleague, and knows perfectly well a co-worker's github handle, it seems convenient to let them say so. Like `knownAs`, this is not making a claim about legal identity; if someone's Twitter handle is @bobTheIncredible, it still doesn't mean that's his name.
There is a final way that the current fields in the schema seem to overlap with what you are imagining, and perhaps this is the one that we should explore further. It is the `basis`field. This field intends to give a verifier some idea how deep the issuer's knowledge is of the issuee. So an issuer that says the basis of their credential is "family" is saying they've known the issuee intimately for years; "colleague" is another fairly strong but slightly different basis; "acquaintance" is the basis that Alice should assert for Bob when she meets him at a conference.
I listed in example values for this field the values "nist-ial2". This would be a basis where someone would have to compare a person's live face to a credential like a passport. So if that basis is claimed, a `machineCheck` *might* make sense. However, I'm still not sure it's optimal, because if a person actually used a machine to check the validity of a passport, I suspect that the person who did this was working for an institution that requires NIST-IAL2 vetting. Thus, the issuer should be an institution rather than a person. That would make this a different credential type -- not person-to-person, but institution-to-person.
What are your thoughts?

If this is case 2, why do we need a separate scheme? These are companies whose business is identification, which means they probably already have a scheme that describes a human being. One or two optional fields can be added to indicate that the person has been identified as a living person.
If case 1
How is the problem solved?
The average person has two levels of reputation.
The first level consists of dozens of social connections that you can trust directly
The second level is the reputation a person creates for himself in the general public through social networks or any other public publication.
If I understand correctly, the solution is intended for applications that want to prevent a non-human entity from registering as a user several times, otherwise, what does it matter if he is a human or a bot?
So the first level is less relevant because it is very limited in scale. This is because the identifier issuer does not have enough reputation for an application to rely on.
On a second level, we transfer enormous power to famous people, whom we can apparently trust if they saw someone they really see (they protect their reputation and do not make money from creating an identity).

I don't think the purpose should contemplate your use case 2 (identification companies) at all. That's because the credential must be issued by a person, not an institution. Identification companies never issue credentials as *individuals*; they issue as *institutions*.
> If case 1... If I understand correctly, the solution is intended for applications that want to prevent a non-human entity from registering as a user several times, otherwise, what does it matter if he is a human or a bot?
This doesn't prevent Sybil attacks, because one person could hold many of these credentials, and register once with each of them. Rather, this prevents an AI or a device from registering AT ALL, and is agnostic about whether a person should be able to register more than once.
But your language presupposes that the verifier of the credential will be an org that needs to register users, and that kind of hides the main use case in my mind: *what if the verifier is an ordinary human?* There might not be any "registration." What if Alice wants to have a private chat with a person she met on the internet, but she wants to make sure it's not a bot? What if an author wants people to give feedback on the draft of his new novel, but only if they are real human beings? (Almost EVERYTHING in SSI right now ignores ordinary people as verifiers. I wrote about this problem here: )
I really like the goal of leveraging “trust that is cheap, common, and neglected by heavier-weight mechanisms”
It seems the hardest part of this credential schema is agreeing on the schema. Adding biometric hashes and confirmed handles, as well as the “basis” field and “caveats” seems too complicated to get started. Great roadmap features, yet so much optionality there, and difficult to constrain without knowing how to limit it well.
I suggest starting with only four attributes. knownAs, minutes, dt (timestamp), and a very constrained “basis” field so that it is easy to use and hard to confuse.
Since the goal is to establish personhood then online handles aren’t really necessary or can be condensed into the knownAs field as a separate credential for each online handle. why not use a multiplicity of credentials? Or just link them as separate credentials in a graph to the base personhood credential?
You could maybe even simplify it to three, known as, minutes, and dt, and then have basis be a separate credential as shown in the following diagram.
With the faceToFaceCredential as the root for a given interaction between two people you can then layer in additional facts as they become relevant to a given relationship. Then, when that relationship is shared with another person, then they can consume as many additional bases or handles as they require to reach a trust assurance level they are comfortable with.
Having multiple bases for the relationship allows it to evolve over time, from a simple name into something more as the story unfolds.
I know it could seem silly to say the original model was too complicated and to then suggest a rather complicated looking credential graph.
The way I see it each individual credential should be simple, representing a specific kind of interaction. You combine many small credentials to make a credential graph of something overall that is larger. This allows you to have fine grained expression of each part of the reputation while keeping each individual action simple and quick.
I like your thinking, Kent. More granular is better WRT credentials.

2023-05-19T11:00:44.000Z
How about this:
RUN off the CRUD.
RUN stands for Read , Update, Nullify. Why is it preferred ('run off') over the CRUD (Create, Update, Delete)?
Consider the need to protect 'authentic data' in a decentralized environment.
In a decentralized control model, the data always originates from a controller (aka client). The data created (sourced) by the controller follows the principle of 'Non-Interactive Replay Monotonicity' to be able to protect the data from a replay (events are changed) or a deletion (some events are deleted) attacks. That is to say, the data (or events comprising it) is never deleted, it's rather always added to via updates. Each update, therefore, forms a verifiable, continuous log ( e.g. by providing growing sequence number, date timestamp, etc for each update). To enable invalidation of data, a special update, called Nullify, is used.
The client, therefore, updates the server (it's peer or peers), which just maintains the log following certain rules (see BADA - Best Available Data Acceptance).
To summarise, the server can only Read the log, add Updates to it, including Nullifying ones. So no Create or Delete.
Great! Thx
I can paste it in, or you can do it an receive the “credits” in the commit message.

2023-05-26T18:08:13.000Z
Here is my mental model for KERI watchers, which may not be accurate.
I would like to separate two cases: (1) controllers are typical end users and (2) controllers are organizations that issue credentials.
For end users, watchers are probably unnecessary most of the time. Alice can send a KEL to Bob and another inconsistent KEL to Cedric without causing any problems. Duplicity would arise only in the case where Bob and Cedric need to exchange their data about Alice. In this scenario, either Bob or Cedric may set up watchers to monitor Alice’s witnesses.
For organizations, they may issue a lot of credentials (ACDCs) to many people, organizations, or even to the public (as untargeted ACDCs). In this case, I believe it is necessary to set up watchers.
I can give an extreme example where a government is behaving duplicitously. In this case, the government’s witnesses are designed to promulgate different KELs to different groups of people.
Let’s say the president of that country issues an (untargeted) ACDC and makes it available to half of its citizens using one version of its KEL. Then, the president uses another version of its KEL that is inconsistent with the previous one to issue another ACDC that is made available to the other half of its citizens.
Without watchers, the citizens might not be able to detect that two inconsistent KELs have been used. The government may also repudiate one of its ACDCs at a later time.
If watchers are available, on the other hand, the citizens will be able to tell immediately that the government is doing something fishy.
This is a good example. This clarifies that watchers ensure that one party cannot tell two different versions of the facts to two different parties about getting caught as long as the two parties check with the same watcher network, or check with each other.
By watchers do you mean witnesses? Duplicity is detected by the witnesses. Then, watchers can validate the KEL and receipts signed by the witnesses to detect misbehavior.
I meant watchers. Is duplicity detected only by witnesses? Or could a controller use two different witness sets to defraud people in a way that would only be detectable by watchers?
ok, you can have two identical witness sets that can be part of the scam. In that case, I agree that watchers can help detect the inconsistencies.
<@U03P53FCYB1> The witnesses are assigned by a controller. My understanding is that a malicious controller can also hack the witness KA2CE protocol such that they behave duplicitously.
I believe the witness KA2CE protocol is only useful when the controller is honest, and some of the witnesses (that are fewer than the BFT threshold) are compromised.
If the controller is malicious, or the witnesses are compromised above the threshold, then watchers are needed to detect duplicity.
Hmm. Controllers publish their witness sets ( OOBI). Each witness maintains a hash linked, witness and controller signed "micro ledger" (aka KEL). Assuming that witnesses are not compromised ( RUN and not CRUD) the duplicity originates from the controller ( it signs all the events in the chain, collects and distributes the witness receipts). In other words, Alice would need to construct completely different versions of the KEL and get its set of witnesses to re-write the history for duplicity to reach the public. If Alice, on the other hand, publishes different sets of witnesses ( not via rotation - it retains history) then it means that there are two version of the Alice's identity in the wild. But these two versions are consistent ( because of the write only KELs).
Watchers can be used to both detect rewritten history (compromised or incorrect witnesses) and verify identity's messages and ACDCs.
Any agent that has to deal with KERI identities ( same as prefixes) has to maintain a local copy of the identity's KEL and watch out for rotation ( rot + drt) and interaction (ixn) events in order to maintain the latest set of keys, backers ( aka witnesses) sets, anchors for delegated identities and TELs.
While doing so, watcher must obtain the logs on periodic basis and compare them against the stored and verified KEL ( first time obtained via OOBI). Store the difference. Due to chaining ( sn + p, p being said of the prev event) any attempt to rewrite history will be detected. At this poin, a watcher can poll other witnesses in the set and thus detect "lying" witnesses or determine that prefix is not trust worthy ( assuming the first OOBI check was performed agains all witnesses).
Furthermore, one can use "first seen replay couples" ( sn + timestamp) to determine the moment in time when the attempts to rewrite history started.

the multisig feature you're looking for, internally employs public keys for signing keys and their digests for rotation keys. You don't need to create any additional identifier, because in the end the multisig feature relies on solely one identifier that just has several members (public keys) and associated thresholds. Actually thanks to recent changes to the protocol, you can establish `personal` , as you call it, identifier, and i.e., two rotations later join more public keys (more devices) into it, making it a group in essence.
user.contact
Right, but this becomes pretty complicated when we scale. What I originally wanted is to have one group identifier that is controlled by n personal identifiers which themselves are controlled by n keypairs.
But it is actually implemented like this: One group identifier is controlled by n keypairs (the group itself does not know which of the controlling keypairs belongs to alice personal identifier and which belongs to bob)
what type of scale problem you have in mind ?
I think in parctice it can become pretty tedious when we generate one keypair per device.
It makes sense to rotate the personal identifier, everytime we add a new device with a new keypair but if the user is a participant in 50 other groups, not only would he need to rotate his prersonal identifier to add the new device keys, he would also need to rotate the other 50 groups he is part of.
Assuming every user stores the kel of every group he is part of, this would mean that every user needs to fetch the new kel for the group, just because one participant of that group added a new device.
In other words, if alice wants to add bob to her multisig, she needs to know all the device keys of bob.
I am searching for a way to achieve some sort of group functionality, where alice only needs to know bobs personal identifier.
And this could be achieved by adding new members as witnesses or delegates instead of rotating them in as actual controllers via their private keys.

Link to paper about saidifying arbitrary document types:
2023-06-27T15:03:53.000Z
I had a similar problem with embedding large image/video files in ADCDs, and I don’t want ACDCs to get too big when they are transmitted around. I really appreciate that you wrote and shared this document.
If you do not mind, I have some dumb questions due to my lack of understanding of how metadata works in typical opaquely-structured-data.
• When an opaquely-structured-data file is saidified, is its metadata also hashed along with its content? — I suppose it is a yes.
• When the SAID is embedded in the filename “q2financials-E2948372a9b9019.docx”, if the filename is changed to, e.g., “report-E2948372a9b9019.docx”, is the SAID still valid? — My understanding is that the SAID must be recomputed if the filename is changed.
• If I understand correctly, the metadata of a file changes when you use it in different operating systems. Would this cause a problem with the saidification if the files must be used in a multi-OS environment?
Hi, <@U04H17ZEX9R>. Believe it or not, I just noticed this now. Sorry to be 2 months late. Wow.
Yes, metadata stored *inside* the file is hashed along with content. But metadata stored *outside* the file (e.g., last mod date, permissions) is NOT hashed.
When SAID is embedded in filename, the SAID does *not* have to be recomputed when the filename changes. The filename is not input to the hash function. Rather, the regex for the filename that's stored inside the file is input to the hash -- and that regex doesn't change when the filename changes. For example, if the regex is `.*{said}\.docx`, then any filename containing the SAID and ending in docx is a valid filename, and nothing needs to be recomputed when the file is renamed.
Re. multi-OS: no, this metadata is not hashed and would not cause a problem.
Thank you so much! I really appreciate the answer.

1. Alice incepts an identifier
2. Bob incepts an identifier
3. Now Alice generates a delegation even that delegates signing authority over her identifier to Bob's identifier
4. Now Bob can sign messages with his identifier on behalf of Alice
2023-07-02T15:53:23.000Z
Additional details:
• In step 2, Bob has to incept his AID in the delegation mode, i.e. specifying Alice’s AID inside his inception event.
• In step 3, Alice anchors Bob’s AID in her interaction event.

How can I pay for a Slack channel setup by someone else?
The payment for a Slack workspace (a collection of channels, direct messages, and the people who belong to them) is typically managed by the workspace owner or an admin. If you want to pay for a Slack workspace that was set up by someone else, here are some general steps you could follow:
1. Contact the Workspace Owner/Admin: Reach out to the workspace owner or an admin to express your intention. They can change billing responsibilities if they agree.
2. Change Billing Ownership: If the current workspace owner or admin agrees, they can transfer ownership to you. This can be done through the workspace settings. Remember, this gives you control over the entire workspace, not just the payment, so it’s a significant responsibility.
3. Add a New Payment Method: Once you’re the billing owner, you can add a new payment method. Go to
4. S`ettings & administration`
5. > `Billing` > `Payment method`.
6. Update the Payment Information: Enter your payment information and make sure it’s set as the default. You will then be billed for the workspace subscription.
Remember, it’s important to discuss these changes with the current workspace owner/admin and other relevant parties to ensure everyone is comfortable with the change. If you’re paying on behalf of a company, it’s also essential to make sure this complies with any relevant policies or procedures your company may have.
Please note that this information is based on Slack’s policies and procedures as of September 2021, so it may have changed. Be sure to check Slack’s current documentation or contact their support for the most accurate and up-to-date information.

Hey everyone, for the next little while I have an hr (ish) daily to start contributing toward a JS/TS library if there's agreement that it's a positive contribution to make at this time. Given the right support in terms of understanding the spec and implementation I'm willing to put some time and effort here.
As a start I began exploring possibility of strong compile-time typings for some of the primitives like identifiers. I quickly ran into TS limitations. For example it's possible to type for a 44 character base64 SAID but it fails with depth of recursion for 512 (88 char) identifiers. We could use Opaque types but it's a bit hacky with TS and you make some downstream trade-off.
I wonder if it makes more sense to expose types best we can for consuming devs via JSDoc / TS definitions while leveraging a validation library like Joi for runtime checks instead of trying to have strict types at the library level. This would also make development more productive imo.
Would love some thoughts on the above. Would also love to have someone to help orient me toward action assuming again that a TS/JS lib is a productive use of effort at this time.

There are several precursors that are required to start that. 2023-08-10T16:56:42.000Z
Sorry, I was referring to core values of SSI. I just assumed that this community shares these values.
I think <@U05DT8YPEG1> raised an interesting point on the value alignment between KERI/ACDC and SSI.
I cannot speak for others in the community about what they think the values of KERI/ACDC and the community are, but for me, KERI/ACDC represents something more foundational than SSI. One can use KERI/ACDC to build either SSI or non-SSI applications/ecosystems.
From the technical standpoint, the core value of KERI/ACDC is in “Authenticity”, that is, to build something with strong secure attribution. Other properties like privacy, confidentiality, and anonymity are important too, but they are not the top priority.
This is quite different from the core value of SSI which emphasizes self-sovereignty, control, and ownership of personal data for individuals.
However, the technical value may or may not reflect the values of members of the community. This might be a good philosophical discussion for the community.
I can share same view from perspective of Human Colossus that protocols behind KERI and ACDC address low level architecture of authenticity in general. We have many applications where those protocols have nothing to do with SSI. It does not mean that you cannot build SSI application but we cannot ignore the existing world which is not SSI driven and won't be for very long time.
In our case we leveraging properties of KERI to provide integrity (SAID) and authenticity (SCID) to lower layers of dynamic data economy stack, You can read more about that in this blog post: and in referenced in that blog post document about DDE
not many people understand bigger picture of accurate data

2023-09-06T09:50:40.000Z
Discussion thread: how to efficiently watch witnesses
2023-09-06T09:50:40.000Z
In Provenant's current command-line wallets, we run `kli local watch` every time we log in. This helps the different members of some of our multisig AIDs catch up if they've missed events since their last login. It works well.
However, I'd like an efficient way to do some more ambitious watching than this -- and that's what this thread is about.
Thing 1 that I'd like to do: `register a webhook with a witness so I can be called back any time ANY KEL/TEL changes`
Thing 2 that I'd like to do: `poll a witness efficiently for all changes in any KEL/TEL since timestamp or state hash X`
I am wondering if either of these things is already supported. If not, <@U024CJMG22J> or <@U024KC347B4>, do you think would the community accept a PR from Provenant adding either or both of these features?
Unlike the `kli local watch` command, the most convenient scope of both of these features would be "all the AIDs the witness services" rather than an enumerated subset of AIDs.
Regarding #1: I don't imagine that registering the webhook has to be exposed to the public over a web service endpoint; I'm rather imagining this as something configured internally by the owner/operator of a witness. Provenant would use it on its own witnesses, because it would make it very easy to discover that a credential has been issued or revoked, or a key has been rotated.
Regarding #2: I'm imagining this would happen over a web service endpoint exposed by the witness, and that it could potentially be called by the public (albeit with optional enforcement of some kind of proof of authorization). Provenant would love to call GLEIF's witnesses periodically over an API like this, making sure that we find out about any noteworthy changes rooted in those witnesses. With this feature, if a scope of "all the AIDs the witness services" is deemed too broad, it could still be useful for the smaller scope of an enumerated set of AIDs.
It is possible that this second feature is the logical inverse of the witness gossip feature that's been long imagined (pull vs. push), and that witness gossip could be implemented atop it (or at least with a lot of common code).
Provenant doesn't need these features in the next 6 weeks, but we probably do need them before the end of the year, so if it's something we need to work on, I'd love to be taught/pointed in the right direction and start the journey. If someone has already implemented part or all of this, or is in the process of doing so, so much the better.
There is no support for callbacks coming out of witnesses. That would be a net new feature.
There is a fairly extensive query API exposed from witnesses (as a matter of fact, `kli local watch` uses it) to support query for current state of an AID, current log of an AID and with parameters like, `sn=?` and `anchor={...}` which will live in the witness until that condition is met or until a timeout is reached. All of these work using a KERI `qry` event and when satisfied, the witness sends back a `rpy` event, so they are asynchronous, not an HTTP interactive API. Also, they all work on only one AID at a time.
If you want to see how it all works, you should start in `Kevery.processQuery` in `eventing.py` in KERIpy. That is called from the parser when a `qry` event is streamed in.
I've spent some time studying. My unfamiliarity with the codebase is a handicap, but I made some progress.
Let me clarify why I want this.
Provenant imagines supporting high-speed signing for millions of brands. These brands will all have a multisig AID, and they will delegate signing authority to a single-sig AID that can be operated by automation at machine speed. Signing an SMS message or similar does not generate an ACDC and is not anchored to the KEL, because the signatures are only relevant for a short lifecycle (e.g., 10 seconds).
All of these brands will want to be able to revoke delegated signing authority with low latency (e.g., a few seconds of reaction time). This means that Provenant needs to know if delegated authority was changed on millions of AIDs, within a few seconds of when it happens. I don't believe it will be practical to monitor individual KELs and poll for changes.
The good news is, 99.9% of these brands should be using Provenant witnesses. If we configure our own witnesses to tell us when the KEL of an AID changes (the new feature I want, not callable over public web interface), we can then call the witness back and get an updated version of the KEL (existing witness feature), very soon after the change occurs. Since most KELs are unlikely to change frequently, we will have the efficiency we need.
It seems to me that what I want might best be hooked up to KeyStateNoticer and WitnessInquisitor in some way. Am I in the right ballpark?
Actually, maybe processEvent in Kevery?

From my research (using chatGPT):
To download images and videos from a Slack workspace, which are not included in the standard workspace history export, you can follow these steps:
1. Use Slack’s API: Slack’s API provides endpoints for accessing files uploaded to your workspace. You can use methods like `files.list` to retrieve a list of file URLs. This requires some programming knowledge and an understanding of working with APIs.
2. Manual Download: If there aren’t many files or if you’re looking for specific ones, you can manually download them. Go to the conversation or channel where the file was shared and click on the file to download it.
3. Third-party Tools: There are third-party tools and services available that can help you download all files from your Slack workspace. These tools usually integrate with Slack and automate the process of downloading files. Be sure to choose a reputable and secure service, as this involves sensitive data.
4. Request Slack Support: If you’re facing difficulties or if your workspace has a large number of files, consider contacting Slack support for assistance. They may be able to provide a solution tailored to your specific needs.
5. Automate with a Script: If you have programming skills, you can write a script using Slack’s API to automate the download process. This could be especially useful if there are a large number of files.

Hello!. I'm making my first steps with keripy. So far so good with the basic
demo scripts :grinning:. I notice that the swagger api exposes a server-sent events method. What
type of notifications are sent to the controller? is there documentation regarding the events? Also,
I see a /notification method, is that for querying same notifications?
2022-10-08T20:40:59.000Z
Hi Rodolfo- We upgraded the SSE endpoint and the notifications recently to
match more of a Firebase approach.
Anything coming over the SSE channel is just a ping to a live client to refresh some other data set.
The Notifications are a persistent dataset that are messages to the controller of an agent to take
some action. They are persistent and need to be managed (marked as read, deleted) by the controller
of the agent.
So right now, the main use of SSE events is to let the controller of an agent know that there are
new notifications and that a client should reload that dataset.
Sadly we have not documented the SSE events yet.

2022-10-12T01:54:52.000Z
The OOBI is the mechanism to allow a controller to associate an endpoint with an AID. It says, "to contact this AID, use this endpoint (tcp or http)". Then any controller that has resolved the OOBI for a witness just needs to specify that witness by AID in it inception event.
2022-10-12T01:57:36.000Z
So client configuration needs to provide the witness OOBIs in keripy configuration to allow the AID -> endpoint association and the client needs to allow the controller of an agent to select the witness by AID. In the Keep for the vLEI ecosystem we provide "pools" of witnesses (by AID) that are collections from the GLEIF provided witness network. The OOBIs are in the agent configuration and the user interface allows the controller to select them by "pool" which puts the AID in the `b` field of the inception event.

2022-10-17T13:34:06.000Z
great. I saw the references in the code but not sure if it was functional. Do all cesr messages go directly to the mailbox and then need to be retrieved and processed?
2022-10-17T14:08:06.000Z
It all depends on what endpoints are exposed via OOBIs. For all of our current samples (in the scripts directory) and our work with the vLEI, we are exposing witness OOBIs from every controller and controller OOBIs from every witnesses. So when I resolve an OOBI for another, non-witness AID I receive the KEL of the controller which provides the cryptographic commitment to the witness and I receive reply messages with provides BADA-RUN data for endpoints for the witness (who has persistent availability on the internet and thus exposes both TCP and HTTP endpoints). Because I do not have endpoints for the AID but I do have endpoints for her witnesses, I have to send messages to the mailboxes on the witnesses to be forwarded to the AID controller. Those messages can be sent to either the TCP or the HTTP endpoint on the witness but for now we are only using HTTP.
Since we are configuring out agents without exposed ports on the internet (or using the command line) we run all agents and command line commands with pollers for their mailboxes. They check all witnesses for any messages that have been forwarded to their AIDs. The pollers pull the messages down and send them through the parser just as if they arrived in any other manner (direct connection via TCP or over HTTP).

> additional optional prefix to file location of KERI keystoreand `hio/base/filing.py` constructs the path as so:
path = os.path.abspath(
os.path.expanduser(
os.path.join(headDirPath,
tailDirPath,
base,
name)))This led me to believe that the `base` attribute was originally intended to be used as an optional segment of the path like so:
`/headDirPath/tailDirPath/base/name`
Because of this code segment in `Filer` I assumed that both `headDirPath` and `base` must be specified together
However, the `existing.existingHby` context manager does not have a property for specifying the configuration directory, headDirPath, which leads me to believe base is being used with an assumption of using the default `HeadDirPath` or `AltHeadDirPath` from the `Keeper` class.

2023-02-02T19:46:49.000Z
I’d like to write a blog post tutorial and video on how to do what would be `kli vc verify` so it is reasonably clear to anyone trying to use KERI how to use it for issuing and verifying credentials.
Here’s the high level overview from what I understand. Please correct me where I am wrong and add any missing parts.
I know Petteri mentioned and it’s only a few hundred lines of code. I haven’t looked into it deeply yet.
From what I understand there are a few things involved:
1. Prefix creation on either side, both controllers A and B
2. pairwise OOBI exchange between controllers A and B
3. VC registry creation for controller A
4. ACDC schema creation by controller A
5. ACDC schema registration by controller A
6. ACDC issuance by controller A
7. ACDC transmission to controller B, which likely triggers a VC registry creation in the Hab if it doesn’t exist yet.
8. ACDC schema discovery by controller B
9. ACDC reception by controller B verifies the credential.
10. ACDC schema validation by controller B
11. ACDC signature verification by controller B
I haven’t looked deeply into the vLEI codebase yet though from what I can tell it is used for some sort of schema registration and discovery.
And if the features don’t exist to do this yet then please post the Github Issues for them so I can know where to focus my efforts. I’m ready to pitch in to build whatever is missing.
